memoryText: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Zechariah 4:6 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse was spoken to a governor who was staring at a mountain. Zerubbabel had laid the foundation of the temple, and for years had been unable to finish it. Armies, kings, and officials stood in the way. Into that situation, God spoke a short sentence.

“Not by might.” The word means an army or a strong force. Zerubbabel might have thought that the solution was more soldiers or more money. God says no. Human resources are not what will finish the temple.

“Nor by power.” The second word means personal strength, ability, or skill. It is not just armies but individuals. Not by his talent, his leadership, or his charisma.

“But by my Spirit.” The third phrase is the answer. The work of God is done by the Spirit of God. This is the oil in the lampstand vision, flowing without human hands. The Spirit gives the energy, the wisdom, and the ability to finish.

“Says the LORD of hosts.” This is the ground of the promise. The LORD of hosts, the commander of heaven’s armies, makes the promise. He can do what armies cannot.

The verse does not say we do nothing. Zerubbabel had to keep building. But the building was to be done in dependence. The result: “He shall bring forward the top stone amid shouts of Grace, grace to it!” When the work is done, the glory goes to God.

Say this verse when you are tempted to rely on your own strength: in a ministry, a marriage, a job, a struggle with sin. It is a reminder that the work belongs to God, and so does the power.
weekInReview: This week you read the prophets of the return. In Haggai, you heard a call to “consider your ways” and to build God’s house first, and you saw the people’s response and God’s promise: “I am with you.” In Zechariah, you read the eight night visions: the man among the myrtle trees, the wall of fire, Joshua in filthy garments made clean, the lampstand fed by the Spirit, and the crowning of the Branch, a priest on his throne. You heard a rebuke of empty fasting and a promise of old men and children in the streets of a restored Jerusalem. Then you read the first oracle, with the humble king on a donkey, the prisoners of hope, and the shepherd sold for thirty pieces of silver. Earlier in the week, Psalm 99 reminded you of the holiness of the God who answers.
reflectionQuestions: Haggai said, “Consider your ways.” What might God show you if you honestly reviewed how you spend your time, energy, and money?
Zechariah showed Joshua cleansed and clothed by grace alone. How does this picture comfort you when you feel unworthy?
The king of Zechariah 9:9 comes humble and on a donkey, yet his rule reaches the ends of the earth. What does that teach you about how God’s kingdom advances?
prayerPrompts: Tell God that it is not by might or power but by his Spirit.
Thank him for the humble King who has come.
Thank him for clothing you in his righteousness.
